# Together KC - Kansas City Earnings Tax Renewal Campaign

## Overview
Together KC is the official campaign supporting the renewal of the Kansas City, Missouri earnings tax (e-tax) in the April 7, 2026 election. This is not a new tax or tax increase - it is a renewal of the existing 1% earnings tax that has been in place since 1963.

## Key Facts

### The Earnings Tax
- Tax Rate: 1% on income earned within Kansas City, Missouri
- In Place Since: 1963 (over 60 years)
- Annual Revenue: $373 million
- Budget Impact: Funds 47% of the city's general fund
- Renewal Cycle: Required by Missouri state law every 5 years

### What the Earnings Tax Funds
- Fire Department and emergency response
- Police Department and public safety
- Emergency Medical Services (EMS)
- Road maintenance and pothole repair
- Trash collection and anti-illegal dumping programs
- Snow removal services
- Parks maintenance

### Who Pays
- Everyone who earns income working within Kansas City pays 1%
- Approximately 50% of revenue comes from non-residents who work in KC but live outside city limits
- Retirees do not pay the earnings tax
- Military personnel on active duty do not pay
- Unemployed individuals do not pay

## 2026 Election Information

### Important Dates
- Election Day: April 7, 2026
- Absentee/Early Voting Begins: March 24, 2026

### How to Vote
- Vote YES to renew the existing earnings tax
- Voting NO would eliminate the tax and 47% of city funding

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Will voting "yes" raise my taxes?
A: No. Voting "yes" simply renews the existing 1% earnings tax at the same rate it has been for over 60 years.

Q: Why is this being put up for a vote?
A: Missouri state law requires cities with an earnings tax to put it up for renewal every 5 years.

Q: Can we fund these services another way?
A: The earnings tax is the most equitable funding mechanism because about half the revenue comes from non-residents who work in Kansas City and use city services.

Q: What happens if the tax is not renewed?
A: The city would lose 47% of its general fund revenue, requiring massive cuts to fire, police, EMS, road maintenance, trash collection, and other essential services.
